aspectTitle: Generic/boilerplate link text with a non-empty name but no purpose, and no context that rescues it (G91/H30 substantive failure)
aspectDescription: A link whose accessible name exists and is non-empty but is generic boilerplate ('click here', 'read more', 'more', 'here', 'details', 'learn more', 'link', 'continue', '>>') or is just the bare URL, AND for which no programmatically determined link context (the same sentence, paragraph, list item, table cell, or associated table-header cell, or aria-label/labelledby/describedby) supplies the missing purpose. The name passes the only APPROVED rule (c487ae) trivially because it is a pure name-presence gate. The judgment is irreducibly semantic: read the link text plus its containing block and d
scenario: Local-newspaper front page: a lead story ends with a paragraph whose entire content is a single link reading 'Read more'. The only descriptive text (the headline) is in a different block (the <h2>), which is not programmatically determined link context.
mechanism:
The link's programmatically determined context is its own

, which contains only the generic phrase 'Read more' with no purpose words; the descriptive headline sits in a separate block and is not same-sentence/paragraph/list-item/cell nor aria-linked, so a screen-reader user on the Links List hears only 'Read more, link' and cannot determine the destination (the F63 adjacent-block condition).

scenario: Electronics shop: the SAME '>>' (raquo) chevron glyph link appears twice. In 'Editor's pick' it sits in the same sentence as a named product ('iPhone 15 Pro >>') and also carries an aria-label — that link PASSES. In 'Also trending' the identical glyph sits alone in its own paragraph with no product name in the block — that link FAILS. One page, opposite verdicts decided only by context.
mechanism: The PASS link's accessible name is 'iPhone 15 Pro details' (aria-label) and is reinforced by the same-sentence product name (G53). scenario: Public-health dashboard: a bar chart of childhood MMR coverage with a <figcaption> ending in a 'learn more' link. The caption sentence names the destination subject ('the methodology and clinic-level breakdown behind this 2025 dip in MMR coverage') immediately before the generic phrase, and the link lives INSIDE the figcaption — the hardest borderline PASS.

aspectTitle: Purpose visible on the page but located OUTSIDE the programmatic link context (F63 — wrong container, including context that follows the link)
aspectDescription: The information needed to understand a vague link IS present and visible — a sighted reader can find it — but it sits in content that is NOT programmatically associated with the link: a different paragraph, an adjacent (non-header) table cell, a different list item, a layout-table row above, or text that FOLLOWS the link in the same visual region. The page LOOKS fine, which is exactly the trap. The judgment requires reasoning about DOM container boundaries (sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell/associated <th>) AND about reading-order direction: Understanding and G53 warn that context which
scenario:
Local-news teaser where the stand-alone 'Read the full document' link sits in its own

, and the clause that names the document ('the proposed fee schedule…') is a separate following

. An em-dash makes the two blocks read as one sentence visually, but the description is outside the link's paragraph AND follows it in reading order — two identical links open two different documents.
mechanism:
The link's accessible name is 'Read the full document' and its containing

holds only the link; the disambiguating clause is in the next sibling

, which is not the link's sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell and is not an ARIA-associated description. The describing text also follows the link in DOM/reading order, so a screen-reader user reading top-to-bottom (or on the Links list) hears 'Read the full document' with no destination, and must leave the link to find the context — the F63 wrong-container failure plus the G53/Understanding ordering hazard.

scenario: A transactional HTML-email layout table (credit-union statement notice). Each document is a bold label row ('June 2025 Account Statement', '2024 Year-End Tax Form (1099-INT)') followed two rows later by a separate <td> holding only a blue 'View' button link. The describing label is in a different row/cell than the link, in a role='presentation' layout table that exposes no structure.
mechanism: The table is role='presentation', so AT exposes no rows/columns/headers — it is pure layout. Each link's accessible name is 'View'; the document name is in an earlier sibling tr>td.label-cell, which (in a presentation table) is not the link's table cell and not an associated <th>, and no aria-label/labelledby ties the button to the label. A screen-reader user on the Links list hears 'View, link' / 'View, link' with no way to tell a statement from a tax form — the canonical F63 adjacent-cell-in-a-layout-table failure.

scenario: An investor-relations 'Events & Presentations' page using a definition list: each <dt> holds a recording title ('Q1 FY2025 earnings call', '2025 Investor Day keynote', 'Q4 FY2024 earnings call') and the matching <dd> holds only a pill-shaped 'Listen' link. Three different recordings, three identical 'Listen' links; the title-to-link relationship is dt/dd, which WCAG's closed list of associated contexts does not include.
mechanism: The link lives in the <dd> with accessible name 'Listen' (the play SVG is aria-hidden) and has no aria-label/aria-labelledby. The describing title is in the sibling <dt>. WCAG enumerates programmatic link context as same sentence/paragraph/list-item/table-cell or associated <th> (or an ARIA property) — a <dt> is none of these, and screen readers do not announce the matching <dt> when focus lands on the <dd> link. The user must leave the link to find the title: F63 via a dt/dd association that is not in the enumerated set.

scenario: A county procurement data table listing solicitations, each with two 'Download' links (Specifications packet vs. Bid Form). The two document columns are distinguished ONLY by a second header-looking sub-row whose cells are <td> styled bold/centered to mimic headers — not real <th> and with no scope — so nothing programmatically associates 'Specifications'/'Bid Form' with the link cells. Six identical 'Download' links.
mechanism: This is a genuine data table (first header row is real <th scope="col">), so AT announces header associations as it navigates cells — but only for actual headers. The 'Specifications'/'Bid Form' labels are tr.subhead > td with no scope and nothing pointing to them via headers, so AT treats them as ordinary data, not the column header for the download cells. On a 'Download' link the announced context is at best the merged real header 'Documents' for BOTH columns, so a spec packet and a bid form are indistinguishable; the disambiguating words exist visually but are not the link's associated header cell — F63. (A real <th scope="col"> sub-row would have passed, which is the boundary.)

scenario: An outdoor-gear e-commerce category grid. Each product card is a flex column with an .info <div> (product name, blurb, price) and a separate sibling .action <div> holding a green 'View' button link. Visually the card reads as one unit, but the product name and the link are in two different sibling <div>s; every link's accessible name is just 'View'.
mechanism: Each link is in <div class="action"> with accessible name 'View'; the product name is in a separate sibling <div class="info">. The card is a plain <div> with no list semantics, no heading inside the link, and no aria-labelledby pointing the <a> at the name — verified at runtime that the link does not share a container with the name. The link's programmatic context is therefore empty ('View'); the visually-adjacent name is programmatically unrelated, so a screen-reader user on the Links list hears 'View / View / View' and must leave the link to learn the product — the visually-adjacent-sibling F63 trap.

scenario: A university LMS course-readings list (BIO 201). Each reading is emitted as TWO separate <li> elements — first an <li class="open"> with only the 'Open' link, then an <li class="desc"> with the chapter title — and a CSS grid positions the title cell on the left and the link cell on the right of the same visual row. On screen it reads 'Chapter 4 … Open' (looks compliant); in DOM/reading order it is 'Open' then 'Chapter 4 …', i.e. the description is a different list item that follows the link.
mechanism: The link's own list item (li.open) contains only 'Open'; the chapter title is in the following sibling li.desc — a different list item, with no ARIA association. Screen readers and the Links list follow DOM order, not the CSS-grid visual order, so the title both sits outside the link's list-item context AND follows the link in reading order. Verified at runtime: per reading the <li> sequence is [open]'Open' then [desc]'Chapter…', and all three links expose the name 'Open'. F63 (wrong container = different list item) compounded by the ordering hazard, with CSS deliberately making the visual snapshot look correct.

aspectTitle: Image/icon/SVG-only links with a non-empty name that misdescribes or fails to convey the rendered glyph's purpose (F89 semantic-mismatch variant)
aspectDescription: A link contains only an image, SVG, or icon-font glyph and DOES have a non-empty accessible name (alt, aria-label, title, or aria-labelledby), so F89's empty-name failure and c487ae both PASS — but the name does not match what the glyph depicts or where the link goes. Examples: a magnifying-glass icon labelled 'image' / 'icon1' / the filename 'search.png'; a social brand glyph labelled the generic 'social'; a printer icon whose alt says 'document'; a hamburger menu whose aria-label says 'logo'; an icon-font link whose accessible name is a literal private-use codepoint that conveys nothing; a b
scenario: SaaS CRM header toolbar of three icon-only links — magnifying glass (aria-label="img_2031", the sprite export id), gear (aria-label="settings.svg", the source filename), envelope (aria-label="link", a scaffold placeholder). Every link has a non-empty, mutually-distinct accessible name so c487ae/F89 pass and axe reports discernible text, but none describes the search/settings/inbox purpose the glyph depicts.
mechanism: Each <a> is in the a11y tree with role=link and a non-empty accessible name from aria-label (inner SVG is aria-hidden). The name is an asset filename / sprite id / placeholder, not the link's purpose, so the purpose cannot be determined from the link text and there is no programmatic context. Name-presence floor met; descriptive limb of 2.4.4 fails.

scenario: Local-news article breadcrumb: an icon link back to the Transit section index renders a LEFT-pointing chevron-plus-shaft (the universal back/previous glyph) via a data-URI SVG, destination /transit/index (where the reader came from). Its img alt is the non-empty word "forward" (copied from a paginator's next-arrow sprite); the visible "Transit desk" caption is aria-hidden, so the link's whole accessible name contradicts the glyph and the destination.
mechanism: The <a> is exposed as role=link with accessible name "forward" (only the img alt contributes; the SVG is via src and the caption span is removed by aria-hidden — confirmed via CDP). A screen-reader user hears "forward" and expects to advance, but the link moves them backward to the index. Present, programmatically-determined name that misdescribes both the arrow's direction and the link purpose: F89's present-but-wrong sibling.

scenario: Developer console API-keys data table with per-row pencil (edit) and trash (revoke) icon links. The custom icon set assigned each glyph a Unicode Private Use Area codepoint and auto-emitted the literal PUA character as the aria-label, so each link's accessible name is a single private-use character (U+E801 for edit, U+E803 for delete) — non-empty but semantically meaningless.
mechanism: Each <a> is role=link with a non-empty accessible name of one PUA character (SVG is aria-hidden — confirmed via CDP: name.value codepoints are U+E801/U+E803). PUA codepoints carry no assigned Unicode meaning, so AT announces nothing useful (silence / "private use area E801" / fallback symbol), yet the link IS named. The trash action is destructive (revoke a key) with no spoken warning. Floor met; purpose undeterminable; 2.4.4 fails.

scenario: RTL Arabic recipe site (lang=ar dir=rtl). In a chicken-kabsa recipe card header, an icon-only link renders a download glyph (downward arrow into a tray) pointing to kabsa.pdf — purpose: save the recipe as PDF. But the CMS template bound the aria-label to the article-title variable, so the link is named "كبسة الدجاج بالخطوات" (the recipe's own name), well-formed meaningful Arabic that describes the article rather than the download action.
mechanism: The <a> is role=link with accessible name "كبسة الدجاج بالخطوات" (confirmed via CDP). A screen-reader user hears the recipe title spoken twice (once as h1, once as this link) with no indication the second is a download control; they cannot tell it saves a PDF. Name present, programmatically determined, linguistically valid, but does not convey the link's purpose (the download action); 2.4.4 fails.

scenario: Boundary PASS control: a municipal transit (Route 12 schedule) utility bar of three icon-only links — house (aria-label="Metro Transit home"), printer (aria-label="Print this schedule"), telephone (aria-label="Call rider services: 311", a tel: link). Each has a non-empty name AND the name correctly describes the rendered glyph and the link's purpose, so the page satisfies 2.4.4.

A screen-reader user can determine each link's purpose from the link text alone. Both the name-presence floor (c487ae/F89) and the descriptive limb of 2.4.4 are met.

aspectTitle: Identical accessible name AND identical context, but the links resolve to genuinely different purposes (fd3a94 equivalence judgment)
aspectDescription: Two or more links on the page share the same accessible name AND the same programmatically determined context, yet lead to different resources serving different purposes — the classic 'three Read more / three Download / two Contact us' problem. The judgment is doubly semantic: (a) are the contexts truly identical, and (b) do the destinations serve EQUIVALENT purposes or genuinely different ones? Equivalent (e.g. the same data offered as PDF/XLSX/CSV) can PASS; genuinely different destinations (chat page vs phone page; sales@ vs support@) FAIL. On a self-contained page this is testable using sa
scenario:
Bakery ordering page: one lead sentence (one

) contains two inline links both named 'order form', one targeting #cake-form (a bespoke priced celebration-cake quote) and one targeting #bread-form (a recurring Saturday bread subscription). Identical accessible name, identical same-DOM-node context, genuinely different on-page purposes resolvable via fragment anchors.
mechanism: Two <a> in the same paragraph have identical accessible name 'order form' and therefore identical programmatically determined link context, but resolve to two #fragment sections that serve non-equivalent purposes (one-off priced cake quote vs recurring bread subscription). The disambiguating words ('for celebration cakes' / 'for sourdough and bread boxes') trail each link and are not part of, nor programmatically associated with, it — so a screen-reader links list yields 'order form / order form' with no way to choose.

aspectTitle: Identical accessible name AND identical context, but the links resolve to genuinely different purposes (fd3a94 equivalence judgment)
aspectDescription: Two or more links on the page share the same accessible name AND the same programmatically determined context, yet lead to different resources serving different purposes — the classic 'three Read more / three Download / two Contact us' problem. The judgment is doubly semantic: (a) are the contexts truly identical, and (b) do the destinations serve EQUIVALENT purposes or genuinely different ones? Equivalent (e.g. the same data offered as PDF/XLSX/CSV) can PASS; genuinely different destinations (chat page vs phone page; sales@ vs support@) FAIL. On a self-contained page this is testable using sa
scenario:
Charity grant-spending page: one sentence (one

) offers the SAME four-row dataset in three takeaway formats, each behind an identical link named 'Download this data' — a PDF, an XLSX and a CSV delivered via self-contained data: URIs. Identical name, identical same-DOM-node context, but the destinations are equivalent (same data, different format). PASS boundary control where the discriminator is purpose-equivalence.
mechanism: Three <a download> with identical accessible name 'Download this data' in one paragraph resolve to three encodings (PDF/XLSX/CSV) of one identical dataset (the CSV data: URI literally encodes the same Food/Fuel/Children/Rent figures shown in the table). Per fd3a94's expectation, links sharing name+context PASS when they resolve to equivalent resources; 'same data, different file format' is the canonical equivalence (mirrored by the Understanding's HTML/PDF/mp3 'list of book titles' example). Every user gets the same content from any link, so each link's purpose — obtain this dataset — is determinable.

aspectTitle: Identical accessible name AND identical context, but the links resolve to genuinely different purposes (fd3a94 equivalence judgment)
aspectDescription: Two or more links on the page share the same accessible name AND the same programmatically determined context, yet lead to different resources serving different purposes — the classic 'three Read more / three Download / two Contact us' problem. The judgment is doubly semantic: (a) are the contexts truly identical, and (b) do the destinations serve EQUIVALENT purposes or genuinely different ones? Equivalent (e.g. the same data offered as PDF/XLSX/CSV) can PASS; genuinely different destinations (chat page vs phone page; sales@ vs support@) FAIL. On a self-contained page this is testable using sa
scenario:
Developer-tools SaaS contact card: one sentence (one

) has two inline links both named 'Email us', the first opening mailto:sales@latchkey.dev (pricing/seats/trial), the second mailto:support@latchkey.dev (production incidents/on-call). Identical name, identical same-DOM-node context, non-equivalent mailto destinations routed to different teams; picking the wrong one sends an outage to the sales queue.
mechanism: Two <a> in one paragraph have identical accessible name 'Email us' (hence identical programmatic context) but resolve to two different mailto recipients (sales@ vs support@) serving different functions. Per fd3a94's assumptions the mailto target (a URL) is not counted as disambiguating context, and the distinguishing clauses ('to talk pricing' / 'if something is broken') trail each link without being associated with it — so a links-list view gives 'Email us / Email us' and the user cannot pick the right inbox.

scenario: Plant-care app pricing table laid out as a CSS Grid: two plans (Sprout $9/mo, Greenhouse $99/mo) side by side, each column ending in an identical 'Buy now' link. Each link sits in its own bare grid cell with NO plan name or price; the $9 / $99 price blocks are in separate grid cells positioned visually above their buttons. Disambiguation is conveyed purely by visual column alignment (verified: buy x-centers 123/549 align under price columns 237/663).
mechanism: Two <a> named 'Buy now' resolve to non-equivalent destinations (#checkout-sprout $9 vs #checkout-greenhouse $99), but each link's programmatically determined link context (its own .buyrow cell) is equally bare — neither cell carries the plan or price, which lives in a sibling .price grid cell (the F63 'context not in the link's sentence/paragraph/cell' trap). Sighted users disambiguate by visual alignment under the price column; AT users get two identical 'Buy now' contexts. Because the page DOES convey the difference visually but not programmatically, fd3a94's 'no visual information' exemption does not apply and it fails.

Spanish-language (lang=es) public health-centre contact page (i18n long-tail): one sentence (one

scenario: Volunteer-run tech conference page (negative control): one paragraph contains two inline links both named 'contact us' in the same sentence-pair, one framed around accessibility needs and one around invoices/VAT receipts. Both point to the SAME #contact section — one shared organiser inbox handling every request (verified: 2 occurrences, 1 unique destination). Looks like the failing duplicate-name pattern but is benign because the destination is one and the same.

The surrounding clauses describe two topics (access vs finance) but both are served by one team at one address, so whichever link the user picks, the purpose (reach the organisers) is satisfied identically and no user is misled.

aspectTitle: Sufficiency of preceding-heading / list-grouping context as the purpose carrier (H80 judgment, including when the heading is NOT the link's context)
aspectDescription: A vague link ('Map', 'Book now', 'PDF', 'Read more') is rescued — or not — by a preceding heading or by the grouping structure it sits in (a section heading above a nav of links, a hotel-block heading, a document offered in three formats under one heading, a card whose <h2> headline is the appended 'Read more' link's group). The H80 judgment is whether the link text combined with that preceding heading describes the purpose, AND whether the heading is genuinely the link's context versus merely visually-above content. This is distinct from F63 (which is about context in the WRONG container) and
scenario: Two conference hotels (Royal Palm, Three Rivers). The H80 hotel-block shape is broken: instead of each hotel heading being followed by its own nav, both descriptions sit on top and ALL booking links are pooled into one shared 'Quick links' bar as a flat <ul>, with two byte-identical 'Map / Photos / Book now' triads separated only by plain-text <li> sub-labels. Repeated identical link sets where context is the sole differentiator — and that differentiator has been severed.
mechanism: The hotel <h2> names are no longer the preceding grouping heading of the links; the links' nearest grouping heading is the generic 'Quick links'. The 'Royal Palm'/'Three Rivers' labels are in separate <li> elements, not the link's list item, so they are not programmatically determined link context. AT enumerates 'Map, Photos, Book now, Map, Photos, Book now' with no way to tie any 'Map' to a hotel.

scenario: A real-estate site lists two properties (14 Maple Court, 8 Birch Lane). Both cards use the H80 grouping correctly in form — an <h2> names the property and the per-listing <nav> is aria-labelledby that heading — but the second card was copy-pasted and its nav still references id='listing-maple' (the FIRST listing). The association is present and resolves, but to the wrong property: present-but-misleading.
mechanism: aria-labelledby='listing-maple' gives the second <nav> the accessible name '14 Maple Court'. aspectTitle: A specific, well-formed link name that contradicts its actual on-page destination (deceptive but descriptive name)
aspectDescription: The link has a clear, descriptive, non-empty accessible name that reads as 'good' in isolation, but it is WRONG about where the link goes. On a self-contained page this is testable when the destination is a same-page #fragment anchor (or a labelled on-page section) whose actual content is verifiable: a 'Read our Privacy Policy' link whose href is '#terms' (a Terms section that exists on the page); a 'Skip to main content' link pointing to '#footer' instead of '#main'; a table-of-contents entry 'Chapter 3: Results' whose anchor actually holds Chapter 5; a 'Basic — $0/mo : Get started' link jump
scenario: Credit-union 'Help & Legal Centre' with on-page #privacy (Privacy Policy), #terms (Terms of Service), #fees sections. The footer 'Legal documents' nav's first link reads 'Read our Privacy Policy' but its href is '#terms' (the Terms of Service). The honest target is #privacy. Specific, well-formed name pointing at a contradictory but real on-page section.
mechanism: Link accessible name 'Read our Privacy Policy' resolves to '#terms', the Terms-of-Service section, not the Privacy Policy at '#privacy'; the name describes the wrong on-page document, so the link's name does not let the user understand its actual purpose/destination.
